title: 22. Interview: Column-Family Databases
summary: Interview Q&A for Column-Family Databases — 14 questions with model answers.
objectives: Answer 14 Column-Family Databases interview questions out loud
Lead with the concept, then a small example, then a tradeoff

sections.title: Conceptual Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. What is the difference between a partition key and a clustering key in Cassandra, and why does the distinction matter?
**Answer:** The **partition key** is hashed (Murmur3 in Cassandra) to determine which node in the cluster owns the row — it controls *data placement* and parallelism. All rows with the same partition key live on the same node (and its replicas), so cross-partition queries require multiple network hops. The **clustering key** determines the *sort order of rows within a partition* on disk — it controls range-scan efficiency. In `PRIMARY KEY ((user_id), show_id, episode_id, watched_at)`, `user_id` is the partition key (in parentheses) and the rest are clustering keys. The distinction matters because every CQL query MUST include the full partition key (otherwise Cassandra cannot route the request without a full cluster scan), and clustering keys then enable efficient contiguous range scans like `WHERE user_id=42 AND watched_at > 1.7B LIMIT 20`. Choosing the partition key is the single most important schema decision in Cassandra: too coarse (e.g., all users in one partition) creates hotspots; too fine (e.g., per-row partitions) defeats clustering scans. The partition key should distribute writes evenly and group together rows accessed together.
**Visual:**
```
PRIMARY KEY ((user_id), show_id, episode_id, watched_at)
             ^^^^^^^^   ^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^^
             partition  clustering keys (sort order within partition)
             key        -> range scans efficient

  Routing:    hash(user_id) % ring -> owns Node B (and 2 replicas)
  Sort:       within Node B, rows for user_id=42 are sorted by
              (show_id, episode_id, watched_at) on disk
  Query:      MUST specify user_id=? (full partition key)
              MAY specify show_id=?, watched_at > ? (clustering range)
```

### Q2. Explain the LSM-tree write path and why it makes column-family stores write-optimized.
**Answer:** A Log-Structured Merge-tree (LSM-tree) write goes: (1) append the mutation to a sequential Write-Ahead Log (CommitLog) on disk for durability — this is sequential I/O, ~100× faster than random I/O on spinning disks and still meaningfully faster on SSDs; (2) insert the mutation into an in-memory sorted structure called the MemTable (typically a skip list or red-black tree). Both operations are O(1) amortized — no read-modify-write of disk pages, no B-tree splits. When the MemTable fills (configurable threshold, e.g., 64MB), it's flushed as an immutable SSTable to disk (sequential write). Reads must consult MemTable + potentially many SSTables, merged by timestamp and filtered by Bloom filters — so reads are slower than writes, but caching (key cache, row cache, chunk cache) bridges the gap for hot data. Background compaction merges SSTables to bound read amplification. The contrast with B-trees (PostgreSQL/MySQL InnoDB) is stark: B-tree writes require read-modify-write of a disk page (random I/O) and split/merge operations. LSM trades read amplification (multiple SSTable reads) for write amplification — for write-heavy workloads like Netflix viewing events (millions/sec), this is the right trade.
**Visual:**
```
LSM-tree write path (Cassandra/HBase/Bigtable):

  WRITE  ----> [1] Append CommitLog (sequential disk, durable)
               [2] Insert MemTable  (in-memory sorted)

  When MemTable fills:
               [3] Flush -> immutable SSTable on disk (sequential write)

  Read path (slower than write):
  READ   ----> [1] MemTable (in-memory)
               [2] Bloom filter (skip SSTables missing the key)
               [3] SSTable index -> partition offset -> disk read
               [4] Merge fragments by timestamp, filter tombstones

  B-tree (PostgreSQL/MySQL InnoDB) contrast:
  WRITE  ----> read page (random I/O) -> modify -> write back (random)
               -> page splits propagate up the tree (write amplification)
```

### Q3. What is a tombstone, and what happens if `gc_grace_seconds` is misconfigured?
**Answer:** A **tombstone** is a deletion marker — when you `DELETE FROM table WHERE ...`, Cassandra/HBase doesn't physically remove the data immediately; it writes a special marker saying "this column was deleted at timestamp T." Reads then filter out any version with timestamp ≤ T. This is necessary because data may exist in multiple immutable SSTables, and physical removal would require rewriting all of them. Tombstones persist until **compaction** physically merges the SSTable containing the tombstone with the SSTable containing the shadowed data, and only after `gc_grace_seconds` (default 10 days in Cassandra) has elapsed since the tombstone was written. The `gc_grace_seconds` window exists to handle **replica lag**: if a replica was down when the delete was issued, it might still have the shadowed (pre-delete) data. When it comes back online, a read-repair or anti-entropy repair will reconcile it — but only if the tombstone still exists somewhere. If compaction dropped the tombstone before the lagging replica was repaired, the lagging replica will resurrect the deleted data on its next read (the tombstone is gone, so the shadowed data looks live again). This is called **tombstone resurrection** and is a classic operational disaster. Mitigation: keep `gc_grace_seconds` longer than your worst-case replica downtime, run `nodetool repair` frequently, and never disable compaction.
**Visual:**
```
DELETE lifecycle:

  t=0    DELETE row X    -> tombstone written (ts=0, val=None)
  t=1    Read row X      -> tombstone filters shadowed data -> empty
  ...
  t=10d  gc_grace_seconds elapsed -> compaction may drop tombstone
  t=11d  Compaction merges SSTables -> tombstone + shadowed data both gone

  DANGER: replica B was down at t=0..11d (missed the delete)
          -> at t=12d, replica B still has shadowed data
          -> if tombstone was already compacted away on other replicas,
             read-repair sees B's data as "newer" -> RESURRECTS DELETED ROW

  Mitigation:
    - run nodetool repair every < gc_grace_seconds
    - keep gc_grace_seconds > worst-case replica downtime
    - never disable compaction (tombstones must eventually be GC'd)
```

### Q4. Compare Size-Tiered (STCS), Leveled (LCS), and Time-Window (TWCS) compaction strategies.
**Answer:** **Size-Tiered Compaction (STCS)** merges SSTables of roughly similar size into a larger one. Pros: low write amplification (each write is compacted ~4 times total). Cons: many similarly-sized SSTables accumulate, so reads fan out to many files (high read amplification); also, a 50% space spike during compaction (must keep both old and new until drop). Best for write-heavy workloads where reads are rare or cached. **Leveled Compaction (LCS)** maintains SSTables in levels: L0 (newly-flushed, overlapping), L1 (≤ size target, sorted runs that don't overlap each other within the level), L2 (10× L1, non-overlapping), etc. Each level is 10× the previous. Pros: reads touch O(1) SSTables per level — much lower read amplification. Cons: write amplification is ~10× higher (each write is compacted many times to climb levels); also more disk I/O. Best for read-heavy workloads. **Time-Window Compaction (TWCS)** buckets SSTables by time window (e.g., 1 hour, 1 day) and only compacts SSTables within the same window. Once a window closes, its SSTables are frozen and never re-compacted with newer windows. Pros: ideal for time-series data where old data is rarely read; minimizes write amplification by avoiding re-compacting old data; tombstones in old windows can be dropped once `gc_grace_seconds` passes. Cons: poor for non-time-series workloads. Netflix uses TWCS for time-bucketed metrics; HBase defaults to STCS or Stripe-compaction; Cassandra defaults to STCS.
**Visual:**
```
                    Write Amp   Read Amp   Space Amp   Best for
STCS size-tiered    LOW (~4x)   HIGH       HIGH (50%)  write-heavy
LCS leveled         HIGH (~10x) LOW (O(1)) LOW         read-heavy
TWCS time-window    LOW         LOW*       LOW         time-series

  STCS:  [S1][S2][S3][S4] (similar size) -> merge -> [BIG]
         many similar-size SSTables -> reads fan out to all

  LCS:   L0:  [s][s][s] (overlapping)
         L1:  [======]  (10x L0, non-overlap within level)
         L2:  [==============]  (10x L1)
         reads touch O(1) SSTable per level

  TWCS:  hour 1: [S1][S2] -> frozen as bucket1
         hour 2: [S3][S4] -> frozen as bucket2  (never merges with bucket1)
         ideal when old data is read rarely (time-series)
```

### Q5. Why does Cassandra not support arbitrary secondary indexes at scale, and what do you do instead?
**Answer:** Cassandra's built-in secondary indexes (2i and SASI) are *local* to each node — a query `WHERE email='alice@x.com'` (without the partition key) broadcasts to every node, each scans its local index, and results are merged. At 100+ nodes this is unworkable: network fan-out, slow responses, coordinator memory pressure. Worse, secondary indexes on high-cardinality columns (email, username) perform terribly because each lookup returns few rows but touches every node. SASI (SSTable Attached Secondary Index) is faster (uses on-disk Bloom-filter-like structures) but still local. The Cassandra community mantra is: **"if you need to query it, denormalize into a dedicated table."** Instead of a secondary index on `email -> user_id`, you create a second table `users_by_email (email PRIMARY KEY, user_id)` and write to both tables atomically (using a batch in CQL). This gives O(1) lookup by email (one partition key lookup, one node). The cost is write amplification (2× writes) and dual-table maintenance, but the read performance is unmatched. Materialized Views (Cassandra 3.0+) automate this but are notoriously buggy and discouraged in production. The pattern is called **query-first schema design**: enumerate every query your app needs, then create one table per query (denormalized, optimized for that access pattern). Netflix has dozens of Cassandra tables for viewing history alone, one per access pattern.
**Visual:**
```
BAD (secondary index at scale):
  SELECT * FROM users WHERE email='alice@x.com'
    -> coordinator broadcasts to 100 nodes
    -> each node scans local index
    -> merge results
    -> O(N_nodes) fan-out, slow, coordinator memory pressure

GOOD (denormalized query table):
  Table 1: users              (PK=user_id)  -- canonical
  Table 2: users_by_email     (PK=email)    -- lookup table
  Write:  BATCH { INSERT users ...; INSERT users_by_email ...; }
  Read:   SELECT user_id FROM users_by_email WHERE email='?' -> O(1)
          then SELECT * FROM users WHERE user_id=?

Cost: 2x writes, dual-table maintenance
Benefit: O(1) lookup, no broadcast fan-out
```

### Q6. How does Cassandra's tunable consistency model work, and what are the trade-offs between ONE, QUORUM, and ALL?
**Answer:** Cassandra is masterless (Dynamo-style) — any node can coordinate a write, which is then replicated to N nodes (replication factor, RF=3 typically). The consistency level (CL) specifies how many replicas must acknowledge before the coordinator returns success. **ONE** — wait for 1 replica ack; lowest latency, but a subsequent read might hit a different replica that hasn't seen the write yet (eventual consistency window). **LOCAL_ONE** — same but restricted to the local datacenter (avoids cross-DC latency). **QUORUM** — wait for `floor(N/2)+1 = 2` of 3 replicas; combined with QUORUM reads (also 2 of 3), guarantees strong consistency because any quorum-read overlaps any quorum-write (at least one replica has the latest). **LOCAL_QUORUM** — quorum in the local DC only (Netflix's default for multi-DC deployments). **ALL** — wait for all replicas; strongest consistency but slowest and unavailable if any replica is down. **SERIAL / LOCAL_SERIAL** — uses Lightweight Transactions (LWT, Paxos-based) for compare-and-set; ~10× slower than normal writes, use sparingly. The trade-off is the classic CAP tension: lower CL = lower latency and higher availability but weaker consistency; higher CL = stronger consistency but higher latency and lower availability. Netflix uses LOCAL_QUORUM for billing (must not double-charge) and LOCAL_ONE for viewing history (a stale read just shows an old "continue watching" entry — acceptable).
**Visual:**
```
RF=3, write to coordinator, replicas A, B, C

  CL=ONE       wait for A ack -> return (fast, may be stale on B,C)
  CL=QUORUM    wait for A+B ack (2 of 3) -> return
  CL=ALL       wait for A+B+C ack -> return (slow, fails if any replica down)

  Strong consistency (R + W > N):
    QUORUM write (2 of 3) + QUORUM read (2 of 3) = 2+2 > 3 -> overlap guaranteed

  Use cases:
    LOCAL_ONE      -> viewing history (Netflix) - stale OK
    LOCAL_QUORUM   -> billing, financial - must read latest
    ALL            -> rarely used; availability penalty too high
    LOCAL_SERIAL   -> compare-and-set (LWT, Paxos) - 10x slower
```

### Q7. Why does HBase guarantee strong consistency per row while Cassandra defaults to eventual consistency?
**Answer:** The architectural difference traces back to their lineage. **HBase** is a faithful Bigtable clone: each row is owned by exactly one RegionServer at a time (single primary), and writes go through that RegionServer which sequences them via the WAL. Reads also go to the same RegionServer. This single-master-per-row model means there's no ambiguity about which replica is authoritative — strong consistency is automatic per row (but a RegionServer failover takes 20-60 seconds while ZooKeeper detects the failure and reassigns the region). **Cassandra** descends from Amazon's Dynamo: masterless, multi-writer, every replica can accept writes, and conflict resolution is by timestamp (Last-Write-Wins) or LWT (Paxos). This makes Cassandra always-writable (any replica accepts writes even if others are unreachable), which is great for availability but introduces replica divergence during partitions (the eventual-consistency window). The trade-off is the CAP theorem in action: HBase chose **CP** (consistency + partition tolerance — failover is slow but data is always consistent), Cassandra chose **AP** (availability + partition tolerance — always writable, but reads may be stale). Netflix picked Cassandra for multi-region active-active (every region accepts writes, even during a region partition), which HBase cannot do natively. Apple's massive Cassandra deployment similarly relies on always-on writes. HBase dominates when per-row linearizability is non-negotiable (Hadoop analytics, financial ledgers) and single-DC is acceptable.
**Visual:**
```
HBase (Bigtable clone, CP):
  Row R -> owned by RegionServer X (exactly one, via ZooKeeper)
  Write -> X only -> WAL -> MemTable -> SSTable (HDFS, 3x replicated)
  Read  -> X only -> always latest
  Failover: RegionServer X dies -> ZooKeeper detects -> reassign region
             to Y (20-60s downtime) -> strong consistency maintained

Cassandra (Dynamo-style, AP):
  Row R -> replicated to nodes A, B, C (any accepts writes)
  Write -> coordinator -> A, B, C (CL controls how many ack)
  Read  -> coordinator -> reads from any CL replicas (may be stale)
  Always writable (any replica up = write succeeds)
  Trade: stale reads possible (eventual consistency window)

  CAP: HBase = CP (consistent, slower failover)
       Cassandra = AP (always on, may be stale)
```

sections.title: Scenario-Based Interview Questions
sections.body:
### Q1. Netflix wants to store viewing history for 200M subscribers, ~10 events/user/day (2B writes/day, multi-region active-active). How do you model this in Cassandra?
**Answer:** Schema: `watch_history (user_id, watched_at, show_id, episode_id, progress, device_id, PRIMARY KEY ((user_id), watched_at, show_id, episode_id))`. `user_id` is the partition key (each user's history lives on one partition, replicated RF=3 in each of 3 regions). `watched_at, show_id, episode_id` are clustering keys sorted descending so the most recent watches come first. Multi-region: keyspace with `NetworkTopologyStrategy` and RF=3 per DC (us-east-1, eu-west-1, ap-southeast-1) — every region can accept writes (LOCAL_QUORUM for billing-critical, LOCAL_ONE for viewing). Reads are O(1): `SELECT * FROM watch_history WHERE user_id=42 ORDER BY watched_at DESC LIMIT 20` returns the user's last 20 watches in single-digit ms because it's a single-partition contiguous range scan. Compaction: TWCS with 1-day windows (old watches rarely re-read, so freezing old SSTables minimizes write amp). Tombstone management: deletes use TTL (e.g., `watched_at` < 90 days auto-expires) instead of explicit DELETE, avoiding tombstone buildup. Anti-entropy: `nodetool repair` runs weekly per node, well within `gc_grace_seconds=10d`. Capacity: 2B writes/day × ~200 bytes = 400GB/day; with 3x replication × 3 regions = 3.6TB/day, 1.3PB/year — large but manageable across 500+ nodes. This is essentially Netflix's actual architecture.
**Visual:**
```
CREATE TABLE watch_history (
  user_id      bigint,
  watched_at   timestamp,
  show_id      bigint,
  episode_id   bigint,
  progress     float,
  device_id    text,
  PRIMARY KEY ((user_id), watched_at, show_id, episode_id)
) WITH CLUSTERING ORDER BY (watched_at DESC, ...);

Keyspace: NetworkTopologyStrategy, RF=3 per DC
DCs: us-east-1, eu-west-1, ap-southeast-1 (active-active-active)
Compaction: TWCS, 1-day windows
TTL: 90 days (auto-expire old watches, avoid tombstones)
Repair: weekly per node (within gc_grace_seconds=10d)

Read:  SELECT * FROM watch_history WHERE user_id=42
       ORDER BY watched_at DESC LIMIT 20  -> O(1) partition + range scan
```

### Q2. Instagram's feed storage: each user has up to 10,000 media_ids in their feed, written by fan-out-on-publish. Why Cassandra over PostgreSQL, and how do you avoid hot partitions for celebrities?
**Answer:** Instagram chose Cassandra for feed storage because: (1) writes dominate (every publish fans out to N followers' feeds — Justin Bieber with 100M followers = 100M writes per post); (2) reads are by partition key only (`SELECT media_ids FROM feed WHERE user_id=? LIMIT 1000`) — no joins, no secondary indexes; (3) multi-datacenter replication (Cassandra NTS) for active-active across Facebook DCs; (4) linear write scalability (add nodes, rebalance ring). PostgreSQL would require sharding by user_id manually and would be CPU-bound on B-tree splits at 100M-write bursts. **Hot partition problem**: Justin Bieber publishes a photo -> 100M fan-out writes to 100M feed partitions. Each partition is on a different node (good — no single-node hotspot), but the *coordinator* doing the fan-out becomes a bottleneck, and reads of Bieber's own feed partition are hot. Mitigations: (1) **async fan-out** via a queue (Kafka/Scribe) — publish goes to a "celebrity feed" topic, workers spread the fan-out across many coordinators; (2) **celebrity special-casing** — don't fan-out for users with >100k followers; instead, on read-time, merge their feed with the celebrity's recent posts (hybrid fan-out); (3) **partition splitting** — for the celebrity's own feed partition, use a synthetic partition key like `user_id:bucket` (e.g., 10 buckets per celebrity) and merge buckets on read. Instagram uses the hybrid approach.
**Visual:**
```
Fan-out-on-publish (normal user, 500 followers):
  Alice publishes photo P
    -> write P to Alice's outbox
    -> fan-out: INSERT feed (user_id, media_id) for each of 500 followers
    -> 500 partitions touched (different nodes) -> parallel

Celebrity problem (Bieber, 100M followers):
  Bieber publishes photo P -> 100M fan-out writes
    -> coordinator bottleneck, takes minutes

  Mitigations:
  [1] async fan-out via Kafka topic "celebrity_feeds"
      workers spread across cluster -> parallel coordinators
  [2] hybrid fan-out (read-time merge):
      don't fan-out for >100k follower users
      on read: fetch user's feed + fetch Bieber's recent N posts + merge
  [3] synthetic bucketing:
      Bieber's feed partition split into 10 buckets (user_id:0..9)
      reads merge 10 buckets (parallel) -> less hot
```

### Q3. A Cassandra cluster has 30% disk overhead from tombstones after a major data deletion (GDPR purge). What went wrong and how do you fix it?
**Answer:** The GDPR purge issued `DELETE FROM user_events WHERE user_id IN (...)` for millions of users, each generating tombstones. The tombstones are accumulating because: (1) `gc_grace_seconds=10d` hasn't elapsed yet — compaction cannot drop them; (2) STCS compaction may have many similarly-sized SSTables that don't get merged often; (3) tombstones can only be dropped when ALL SSTables containing both the tombstone and the shadowed data are compacted together (a "tombstone-compacting" event), and if the data is spread across many SSTables that don't get picked together, they linger. **Fix**: (1) **run `nodetool compaction`** to force a major compaction on the affected tables — this rewrites all SSTables into one, dropping eligible tombstones (those past `gc_grace_seconds`); (2) **switch to TWCS** if the data is time-bucketed (set `compaction_window_size=1` and `compaction_window_unit=DAYS`) — old time windows compact independently; (3) **use TTL instead of explicit DELETE** going forward — TTL'd data is dropped by compaction without tombstones, avoiding the issue entirely; (4) **verify repairs are running** — `nodetool repair` must run within `gc_grace_seconds` to ensure all replicas see the tombstones before they're dropped; (5) **tune `tombstone_threshold`** (default 0.2 = 20%) — when a single SSTable exceeds 20% tombstones, Cassandra forces a single-SSTable compaction to drop them; lowering this can help. Monitor `nodetool compactionstats` and `sstabledump` to verify tombstone counts. Post-fix: switch future purges to TTL-based expiry and run weekly repairs.
**Visual:**
```
Diagnosis:
  nodetool compactionstats -> many SSTables with high tombstone ratio
  sstabledump X.db -> "Tombstones: 35%" (above 20% threshold but
                       only dropped when ALL shadowed data compacts)

Fix sequence:
  [1] nodetool compact keyspace user_events   (force major compaction)
       -> rewrites all SSTables -> drops tombstones past gc_grace_seconds
  [2] ALTER TABLE ... WITH compaction = {
        'class': 'TimeWindowCompactionStrategy',
        'compaction_window_unit': 'DAYS',
        'compaction_window_size': '1'
      };
  [3] Future purges: use TTL (auto-expire, no tombstone)
       INSERT ... USING TTL 7776000;  (90 days)
  [4] nodetool repair -pr keyspace user_events  (weekly, per-range)
  [5] Monitor: nodetool compactionstats + sstablemetadata

Prevention:
  - prefer TTL over DELETE for time-bounded data
  - tune tombstone_threshold (default 0.2) if needed
  - TWCS for time-series, LCS for read-heavy, STCS for write-heavy
```

### Q4. You're migrating a PostgreSQL sharded-by-user_id messaging app to Cassandra for higher write throughput. What are the top 3 schema-design pitfalls to avoid?
**Answer:** **Pitfall 1: Modeling Cassandra tables like PostgreSQL tables.** PostgreSQL encourages normalized schemas with joins; Cassandra forbids joins and requires one table per query. If you naively port a `messages` table with foreign keys to `users` and `threads`, you'll discover you can't do `SELECT m.*, u.name FROM messages m JOIN users u ...`. Fix: enumerate every query the app issues, then create one denormalized table per query — `messages_by_thread`, `threads_by_user`, `messages_by_user`, etc. Write to all of them atomically via a CQL `BATCH` (or accept eventual consistency). **Pitfall 2: Choosing the wrong partition key.** If you use `thread_id` as the partition key for `messages_by_thread`, a hot thread (group chat with 1000 active users) creates an unbounded partition that overwhelms a single node. Fix: cap partition size — use composite partition keys (`(thread_id, bucket)` where bucket is `message_id % 10`), or archive old messages to a cold table. Also avoid monotonically increasing partition keys (timestamps, auto-increment IDs) — they create a hot shard on the latest token range. **Pitfall 3: Unbounded partition growth.** A user with 10 years of messages in one partition eventually exceeds the recommended 100MB/partition limit, causing slow reads and repair failures. Fix: use time-bucketed partition keys (`(user_id, yyyy_mm)`) or TTL-based expiry for old messages. Netflix's Cassandra viewing-history table uses TTL + TWCS for exactly this reason.
**Visual:**
```
Pitfall 1: SQL mindset
  PG:   messages(id, sender_id, receiver_id, thread_id, body)
        SELECT m.*, u.name FROM messages m JOIN users u ON ...
  -> Cassandra CANNOT join. Create:
     messages_by_thread (thread_id, sent_at, message_id, sender_name, body)
     -- denormalized: sender_name copied in (write-time denormalization)

Pitfall 2: bad partition key
  BAD:  PRIMARY KEY ((thread_id), sent_at)
        -> hot thread (group chat 1000 users) -> 1 partition, 1 node hotspot
  GOOD: PRIMARY KEY ((thread_id, bucket), sent_at)
        -> 10 buckets per thread -> spread across 10 nodes

Pitfall 3: unbounded growth
  BAD:  PRIMARY KEY ((user_id), sent_at)  -> 10y of msgs in 1 partition
        -> exceeds 100MB/partition, slow reads, repair fails
  GOOD: PRIMARY KEY ((user_id, yyyy_mm), sent_at)  -> monthly buckets
        + TTL 1 year (auto-expire old messages, no tombstones)
```

### Q5. Apple runs a 75,000-node Cassandra cluster for messages. How do they handle node failures, topology changes, and cluster-wide repairs without downtime?
**Answer:** At 75,000 nodes, individual node failures are constant — statistically several nodes are always down. Cassandra handles this natively: **(1) Masterless architecture** — no single coordinator; any node can coordinate, and lost coordinators are simply replaced by clients retrying on another node. **(2) RF=3 replication** — every write goes to 3 replicas; CL=LOCAL_QUORUM tolerates 1 replica failure per partition. **(3) Hinted Handoff** — if a replica is down during a write, the coordinator stores a "hint" (the mutation) locally for up to 3 hours (`max_hint_window`); when the replica returns, the hint is delivered. **(4) Read repair** — on reads, if replicas return divergent data, the coordinator repairs the lagging replica in the background (only for CL < ALL). **(5) Anti-entropy repair** — `nodetool repair` runs incrementally per token range (`-pr` flag = parallel, paritioned range) on a rolling schedule (e.g., sub-range by sub-range across weeks) to catch any divergence that hinted handoff or read repair missed. **(6) Topology changes** — adding nodes uses `nodetool bootstrap` (new node joins the ring, streams its token ranges from existing replicas, then serves traffic); removing nodes uses `nodetool decommission` (node streams its data to replicas taking over its ranges, then leaves). **(7) vnodes (virtual nodes)** — by default 256 vnodes per physical node, so adding/removing a node affects a small slice of every other node's ranges (parallel streaming, no single donor bottleneck). Apple also runs sub-clusters per region to bound failure domains and uses LWT sparingly (Paxos at 75k nodes would be catastrophic). The pattern: design for constant partial failure, embrace eventual consistency, automate everything.
**Visual:**
```
75,000-node Cassandra cluster - failure handling:

  Node X dies (happens constantly at this scale)
    [1] Hints: coordinators stored hints for X (up to 3h)
    [2] Quorum: writes still succeed (2 of 3 replicas up = QUORUM)
    [3] Reads: coordinator skips X, reads from other replicas
    [4] Repair: nodetool repair -pr (incremental, sub-range) reconciles

  Topology change (add 1000 nodes for capacity):
    [1] Bootstrap: new node joins ring, claims vnodes (256 per node)
    [2] Stream: parallel streams from existing replicas (vnodes spread load)
    [3] Serve: new node takes reads/writes once streaming completes

  Repair strategy:
    - sub-range repair weekly per range (parallel, -pr flag)
    - completes full ring within gc_grace_seconds (10d)
    - read-repair handles hot partitions opportunistically
    - hinted handoff handles short outages (<3h)

  vnodes: 256 per physical node
    -> adding 1 node affects 256 small slices across cluster
    -> no single-donor bottleneck (parallel streaming)
```

### Q6. WhatsApp stores 100B messages/day across Cassandra. How do they keep write latency under 5ms at that volume?
**Answer:** WhatsApp (and their parent Facebook's messaging infrastructure) achieve sub-5ms writes through several layers: **(1) Schema design** — messages partitioned by `(conversation_id, yyyy_mm)` so each conversation's monthly messages fit in one partition (bounded size, fast reads); clustering by `message_id` (timeuuid) gives chronological order. **(2) RF=3 with LOCAL_ONE consistency** — only one replica ack required, in the local DC; cross-DC replication is async. This minimizes write latency (no quorum wait) at the cost of eventual consistency (acceptable for messaging — a slightly stale read on a replica just shows the message a moment later). **(3) CommitLog on SSD + MemTable in RAM** — writes are sequential I/O (WAL append) + in-memory insert, both O(1). The MemTable flushes asynchronously to SSTables; backpressure only kicks in if MemTables back up. **(4) Tuned JVM** — Cassandra on Java means GC pauses can spike latency; WhatsApp uses G1GC with tuned heap (~16GB; larger heaps have worse GC), and uses off-heap buffers for network and chunk cache to reduce GC pressure. **(5) No LWT** — Paxos-based lightweight transactions are 10× slower; WhatsApp designs schemas to avoid compare-and-set (using timeuuid conflict resolution instead). **(6) Co-located coordinators** — the application servers run in the same DC/rack as the Cassandra nodes they write to, minimizing network hops. **(7) Compaction tuning** — TWCS with hourly windows (messages are time-series), so old data is frozen and never re-compacted, minimizing background I/O during peak. **(8) Backpressure** — if MemTable flush can't keep up, Cassandra rejects writes with `WriteTimeoutException` rather than letting latency spike to seconds; the app retries with exponential backoff.
**Visual:**
```
WhatsApp: 100B msg/day, <5ms write latency

  Schema:  messages ((conversation_id, yyyy_mm), message_id, sender, body)
           -> bounded partition size, chronological clustering
           -> timeuuid message_id (no LWT needed for ordering)

  Write path (sub-5ms):
    app server -> coordinator (local DC) -> 1 replica ack (LOCAL_ONE)
    [1] append CommitLog (SSD, sequential I/O)    ~0.5ms
    [2] insert MemTable (in-memory)                ~0.1ms
    [3] ack to app                                 (cross-DC async)
    Total: ~1-3ms p99

  Tuning knobs:
    - LOCAL_ONE (not QUORUM) -> 1 ack, low latency
    - JVM G1GC, 16GB heap (avoid large-heap GC pauses)
    - off-heap chunk cache + network buffers (reduce GC pressure)
    - TWCS hourly windows (old data frozen, no re-compaction)
    - co-located app + Cassandra (minimize network hops)
    - NO LWT (Paxos = 10x slower)
    - backpressure: reject writes if MemTable backs up (not spike latency)
```

### Q7. You need strong consistency for a banking ledger in a multi-region deployment. Is Cassandra the right choice, and if not, what would you use?
**Answer:** Cassandra is the **wrong choice** for a banking ledger requiring multi-region strong consistency. Cassandra's AP design (always-writable, eventual consistency) means: (1) LWT (Lightweight Transactions) provide linearizability but use Paxos over 4 round trips per write — at ~30ms p99 per write in a single DC, ~100ms+ cross-DC, throughput tanks (single-digit thousands of TPS cluster-wide, not per partition); (2) multi-region LWT would route Paxos through a single coordinator, serializing all global writes; (3) financial ledgers cannot tolerate the LWT failure modes (Paxos quarum unavailability = write rejection). **Better choices**: **(A) Google Cloud Spanner** — globally distributed, externally consistent (TrueTime + 2PC across Paxos groups), ACID transactions across regions, used by financial services; cost is high but correctness is guaranteed. **(B) CockroachDB** — open-source Spanner-like, geo-distributed, serializable isolation, PostgreSQL wire protocol; runs on any cloud. **(C) Amazon Aurora Global Database** — single-writer-per-region (or use multi-writer with conflict resolution), strong consistency within a region, async replication across regions with RPO < 1s; for true multi-writer strong consistency use Aurora Multi-Master (limited). **(D) PostgreSQL with synchronous streaming replication within a region + Bucardo/Logical replication cross-region** — strong consistency in primary region, eventual cross-region. For a banking ledger, the canonical pattern is: **single-writer-per-account** (use a routing layer to pin each account to a primary region) + **CockroachDB or Spanner** for global redundancy. The CAP trade is unavoidable — strong consistency requires either accepting unavailability during partitions (CP) or paying for TrueTime-style external consistency infrastructure. Banks accept this because consistency > availability for money.
**Visual:**
```
Banking ledger: STRONG CONSISTENCY required, multi-region

  Cassandra?  NO.
    - AP design (always-writable, eventual consistency)
    - LWT (Paxos) for linearizability: 4 round trips, 30ms+ p99
    - multi-region LWT: serializes through one coordinator, throughput tanks
    - failure mode: Paxos quorum unavailable = write rejected

  Better choices (CP systems):
  [1] Google Spanner  - TrueTime + 2PC across Paxos groups
                        externally consistent, ACID, global
  [2] CockroachDB     - open-source Spanner-like, PostgreSQL wire
                        serializable, geo-partitioning
  [3] Aurora Global   - single-writer per region, async cross-region
                        RPO < 1s (eventual cross-region)
  [4] PostgreSQL + sync replica + logical replication cross-region

  Canonical banking pattern:
    single-writer-per-account (routing layer pins account -> primary region)
    + CockroachDB or Spanner for global redundancy
    + CAP trade: accept unavailability during partitions (CP) for money

  Rule: consistency > availability for money
```

quiz.explanation: tombstone** is a deletion marker — when you DELETE FROM table WHERE ..., Cassandra/HBase doesn't physically remove the data immediately; it writes a special marker saying "this column was deleted at timestamp T." Reads then filter out any version with timestamp ≤ T. This is necessary because data may exist in multiple immutable SSTables, and physical removal would require rewriting all of them.
